newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Africans seek to reverse brain drain.
newsitem.headline: Africans seek to reverse brain drain.

text.p: African intellectuals and professionals meeting in Ivory Coast have decided to try to reverse the continent's brain drain -- but first they need to find out just how many people are involved.
"I have no figure. We are completely clueless," Jean-Paul Tedga, director of the Paris-based monthly review, Afrique Education, told Reuters during a three-day symposium that ended on Friday.

The symposium, organised by Tedga and grouping French-speaking Africans in Ivory Coast's commercial capital Abidjan, agreed to press for a census of Africans living abroad and a specialised body to carry it out.
"We must know who is who, who is where, and who is doing what," Tedga said.

But delegates said it was important that Africans abroad, who figure prominently among expulsions of illegal immigrants by countries such a France, should realise that the census was not an attempt to track them down and force them to go home.
The aim, they added, was to identify suitably qualified Africans to fill specific jobs back home on the continent as economies expand aand opportunities increase.

Former Organisation of African Unity secretary-general, Ide Oumarou, told the symposium the U.N. Educational, Scientific and Cultural organisation estimated that 30,000 Africans with higher university degrees such as Phds lived outside the continent.
He said the European Union was critical that 25,000 Africans who benefited from scholarships there had not returned home.

"No census has ever been taken showing the exact number of Africans going abroad each year," he said. "African states must set up census units to keep track of the number of Africans leaving the continent."elegates noted that since many African countries won independence in the 1960s tens of thousands of their best educated young men and women had left in search of a better life outside the continent -- whether in Europe or the Americas.

The symposium, in a closing statement, called for a summit of African heads of state in Abidjan in 1998 on the problem and they asked Ivorian President Henri Konan Bedie to lobby other leaders on their behalf.
